pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 60: Growing: pea (flowering!). Bad news: a notice.*

The pea flower opened on a Tuesday, unfolding a center the color of a bruised plum. It was no bigger than my thumbnail, and I had measured it every day for sixty days, writing the numbers in my logbook with a precision that made my hand ache.

Theo and Yusuf were there, and we stood in a tight circle around one small flower, silent. It felt like a christening, except nobody was holding a baby and we were all holding our breath.

Yusuf leaned in until his nose was almost touching the petals. He did not sneeze. This was a miracle.

Gherkin stretched his neck out from the moss, looking at the flower, then at us.

"Mm," he said. "Nicely done."

I wanted to jump, or spin in a circle, but instead I took my tape measure out of my jacket pocket and measured the stem again. Fourteen centimeters. I wrote it down, and I would do it again tomorrow, and the day after that.
pages.image: Three children stand in a tight circle around a small white pea flower with a blue center; a thin girl with glasses and a denim jacket holds a tape measure, a boy in a beanie leans forward, and a small boy with missing teeth peers closely; a mossy tortoise watches from the grass.

pages.text:
On the way home, the car park was full of people. Not cars, but people. They stood in clusters around the door of Block C, their faces turned toward the glass. The air smelled of wet wool and anxiety.

I pushed through the crowd, my backpack banging against my hips. A woman in a yellow coat held a clipboard. She was pointing at something on the door. I stopped.

The notice was bright yellow, stuck to the glass with four silver pins. The heading was bold: GREENFIELD HOMES PLC. Below it, in smaller, colder letters, was the title: LOWELL COURT REGENERATION SCHEME.

I read the first line. My eyes slid over the words, trying to skip them, but they refused to move. The land to the rear of the loading bays was to be sold. Cleared.

A forty-space car park. Work to begin this time next year.

The woman in the yellow coat turned. She did not look at me. She looked at the crowd, as if checking that everyone had read it yet.
pages.image: A crowd of adults in winter coats gathers around a concrete building entrance, looking at a notice on the glass door; a thin girl with brown skin and round glasses stands at the edge of the group, holding her backpack, looking up at the door with a worried expression.

pages.text:
I read it three times. The phrase "derelict land" made my hands shake. I wanted to throw a bin at the wall. I wanted to throw the notice off the door and rip it into confetti.

"Derelict," I said. My voice was too loud. "It is not derelict."

"Hm," said a voice at my elbow.

Mrs. Ilves stood there, her knitting needles still, her grey scarf wrapped tight around her neck. She did not look at the notice. She looked at me. Then she looked back at the glass.

Around us, the neighbors were talking. A man was complaining about the noise of the drills. A woman was counting the spaces. "One hundred and forty," she said, as if the number were a personal insult.

Nobody was asking what was behind the fence. Nobody had asked, because nobody had looked. They were angry about the parking, the dust, the change. But they were not angry about the loss. They did not know there was anything to lose.

I touched the glass, right over the word "cleared." It was cold.
pages.image: A group of concerned neighbors in winter clothes stand in a concrete courtyard, murmuring and pointing at a door; an old woman with a grey scarf stands near a thin girl with glasses, both looking at the glass with serious, quiet faces.

pages.text:
The garden was quiet when I arrived, the wind having dropped until the pear tree leaves hung perfectly still. I sat on the bench that usually hums, though today it remained silent, just a slab of wood waiting for me to make something happen.

I told Gherkin everything. I recited the yellow paper, the phrase "derelict land," and the number one hundred and forty spaces. I described the woman with the clipboard and the way the neighbors complained about the drills instead of asking what was behind the fence.

Gherkin did not say "Mm."

He sat on a large flat stone, his head resting heavily on his front legs, his eyes closed or perhaps just moving very, very slowly. I counted the seconds, one, two, three, continuing until I reached eighty, then four hundred and eighty.

Eight minutes passed.

Then he opened one eye, looking at me with a slowness that felt like watching a single snowflake melt on a hot sidewalk.

"The last line," he said, his voice sounding like dry leaves scraping across stone. "Was true."

I frowned, tilting my head. "Which line?"

"The one about speaking," he said. "Someone must speak for it, when the day comes." He blinked, once, very slowly. "It appears the day is this one."
pages.image: An old tortoise with a mossy shell sits on a large grey stone in a garden, looking up at a thin girl with brown skin, glasses, and a denim jacket who is kneeling on the grass, looking concerned and serious.

pages.text:
"I can't," I said, my voice coming out small and flat. "I am terrible at speaking. I have never put my hand up in a class. I freeze, forget what I am going to say, and sound like a robot that has been programmed to panic."

Gherkin watched me. He did not offer comfort, nor did he offer a plan. He simply watched, with the patience of a creature that had outlived several civilizations, his head resting heavily on his front legs.

"Mm," he said. "Not... yet."

I waited for him to explain, for the "not yet" to mean "no," or for him to tell me to go away and hide in a box. But he just kept watching. Slowly, the tight knot in my chest began to loosen. It did not disappear. It just changed shape, becoming a question instead of a wall.

"Not yet," I repeated, testing the words.

I looked at the pea plant. Fourteen centimeters. Sixty days. It had not hurried, nor had it hidden. It had just grown, one centimeter at a time, until it could open its flower to the world. Maybe I could learn that too.
pages.image: A thin girl with brown skin, round glasses, and a green pencil in her hair sits on a wooden bench in a garden, looking at a small pea plant with a white flower; an old tortoise sits nearby on a stone, looking at her with calm, steady eyes.
